entries.topicDescription: Practical hardening techniques for authentication, storage, network, and runtime protection on Android.

tips.title: Store secrets with Keystore-backed encryption, not plain SharedPreferences
tips.content:
Plain SharedPreferences are readable on any rooted device and are backed up
by default unless explicitly excluded, so tokens stored there can leak.

Use EncryptedSharedPreferences or DataStore with a key wrapped by the Android
Keystore (AES/GCM). The Keystore key material never leaves secure hardware
(StrongBox or TEE when available), so even a rooted attacker can't extract
the raw key — only misuse the app while it's running.

For multi-account apps, prefix keys per account rather than using one shared
file, so tokens don't leak across account switches.
tips.codeSnippet:
val masterKey = MasterKey.Builder(context)
    .setKeyScheme(MasterKey.KeyScheme.AES256_GCM)
    .build()

val encryptedPrefs = EncryptedSharedPreferences.create(
    context,
    "secure_prefs",
    masterKey,
    EncryptedSharedPreferences.PrefKeyEncryptionScheme.AES256_SIV,
    EncryptedSharedPreferences.PrefValueEncryptionScheme.AES256_GCM
)

tips.title: Pin certificates, but always ship a backup pin
tips.content:
Certificate pinning stops MITM attacks even when a trusted CA is compromised
or a malicious profile is installed on the device.

But pinning only the leaf certificate is fragile — cert rotation on the
server will hard-break your app for every user until they update. Pin the
intermediate or a backup public key alongside the primary one, and always
include a pin-validation failure path that fails closed (block the request)
rather than silently falling back to unpinned trust.
tips.codeSnippet:
val certificatePinner = CertificatePinner.Builder()
    .add("api.example.com", "sha256/AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA=")
    .add("api.example.com", "sha256/BBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBB=") // backup pin
    .build()

val client = OkHttpClient.Builder()
    .certificatePinner(certificatePinner)
    .build()

tips.title: Use PKCE for OAuth2 on mobile — never embed client secrets
tips.content:
Mobile apps are public clients: any "secret" baked into the APK can be
extracted via decompilation (JADX makes this trivial), so the classic
authorization-code-with-client-secret flow isn't safe on-device.

PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange) replaces the static secret with a
dynamically generated code_verifier/code_challenge pair per auth attempt,
so even if the authorization code is intercepted, it can't be redeemed
without the original verifier held only in the app's memory.
tips.codeSnippet:
val codeVerifier = generateRandomString(64)
val codeChallenge = codeVerifier.sha256().base64UrlEncode()

// Authorization request
val authUrl = "$authEndpoint?response_type=code" +
    "&client_id=$clientId" +
    "&code_challenge=$codeChallenge" +
    "&code_challenge_method=S256"

// Token exchange includes the original verifier, never the challenge
val tokenRequestBody = mapOf(
    "grant_type" to "authorization_code",
    "code_verifier" to codeVerifier
)

tips.title: Combine multiple signals for root detection, not a single check
tips.content:
Checking for su binaries or test-keys alone is trivially bypassed by Magisk
Hide or similar tools. Treat root detection as a risk score, not a boolean.

Combine filesystem signals (su paths, busybox, Magisk app package), runtime
signals (ptrace detection, unexpected native library presence), and the Play
Integrity API's device/app integrity verdicts. Weight Play Integrity highest
since it's backed by hardware attestation and much harder to spoof than
local checks.
tips.codeSnippet:
fun computeRiskScore(): Int {
    var score = 0
    if (hasSuBinary()) score += 20
    if (hasMagiskApp()) score += 20
    if (isDebuggerAttached()) score += 15
    if (playIntegrityVerdict != MEETS_DEVICE_INTEGRITY) score += 40
    return score // threshold decides block/warn/allow
}

tips.title: Validate JWTs by signature and claims — never trust decoding alone
tips.content:
Base64-decoding a JWT to read its payload proves nothing about authenticity;
anyone can craft a token with an arbitrary payload. The client must verify
the signature against the issuer's published JWKS, and check exp, nbf, iss,
and aud claims before trusting any value in the token.

On Android, prefer validating tokens server-side wherever possible — if the
client must validate locally (e.g. for offline gating), cache the JWKS with
a short TTL and fail closed if the keys can't be refreshed.

tips.title: Single-flight token refresh to avoid a refresh-token race
tips.content:
When multiple requests hit a 401 simultaneously, each naively triggering its
own refresh call causes a race: the first refresh invalidates the old refresh
token while others are still using it, logging the user out unexpectedly.

Guard the refresh call with a mutex or a shared in-flight Deferred so
concurrent 401s await one refresh instead of firing several, and queue the
original requests to retry once the new token is available.

tips.title: Encrypt local databases holding sensitive data with SQLCipher
tips.content:
Room's default SQLite storage is unencrypted on disk — on a rooted or
physically compromised device, cached tokens, PII, or transaction history
in the local DB are readable directly from the file system.

Use SQLCipher's Room integration (net.zetetic:android-database-sqlcipher)
to transparently encrypt the database file with a key derived from the
Keystore, so the on-disk .db file is unreadable without the running app's
key material.
tips.codeSnippet:
val passphrase = SQLiteDatabase.getBytes(keystoreDerivedKey.toCharArray())
val factory = SupportFactory(passphrase)

val db = Room.databaseBuilder(context, AppDatabase::class.java, "secure.db")
    .openHelperFactory(factory)
    .build()

tips.title: Don't rely on obfuscation alone — pair it with runtime integrity checks
tips.content:
Obfuscation (DexGuard/R8) raises the cost of static analysis but does
nothing to stop a repackaged or tampered APK from running once decompiled
and reassembled.

Add runtime integrity checks: verify the app's signing certificate hash at
startup, check Play Integrity's appIntegrity verdict, and detect debugger/
Frida attachment. Treat obfuscation as raising the bar for reverse engineers
and runtime checks as catching the ones who get past it.

tips.title: Scope Android permissions to the moment they're needed
tips.content:
Requesting all permissions (camera, location, storage) at first launch
inflates your attack/privacy surface and triggers user distrust — many
users deny blanket up-front prompts on principle.

Request permissions contextually, right before the feature that needs them
runs, and check shouldShowRequestPermissionRationale to explain why before
re-prompting. This also reduces the app's exposure if a permission is
misused by a compromised dependency, since it's not granted until needed.

tips.title: Never log sensitive data, even at debug level
tips.content:
Debug logs are easy to forget about and often ship in release builds via
misconfigured build variants, or get captured by crash reporting tools that
scrape logcat. Tokens, PII, or full request/response bodies in Log.d calls
can leak through bug reports, ADB access, or third-party SDKs that read logs.

Strip logging in release builds via R8/DexGuard rules that remove Log calls
entirely, and for anything that must log request details in debug builds,
redact sensitive fields before logging rather than trusting build-variant
gating alone.

tips.title: Pin the public key (SPKI hash), not the whole certificate, to survive renewal
tips.content:
Pinning the full certificate's hash means the pin breaks the moment the
certificate is renewed, even if it's renewed with the exact same key pair
— a routine, non-security-relevant renewal forces an app update just to
keep working.

Pinning the Subject Public Key Info (SPKI) hash instead pins the
underlying public key, which stays the same across a routine certificate
renewal as long as the key pair itself isn't rotated — this is what
OkHttp's CertificatePinner and Network Security Config's pin-set both
actually pin against by default, not the full certificate.

tips.title: Declare pins declaratively via Network Security Config's <pin-set>
tips.content:
OkHttp's CertificatePinner requires pins to be compiled into your app's
Kotlin/Java code, which means every pin change requires a full code
change and app release cycle.

Network Security Config's <pin-set> element declares pins in XML instead
— functionally equivalent for enforcement purposes, and it has the added
benefit of applying at the OS level, so it protects any networking
library and even WebView traffic within your app, not just requests made
through a specific HTTP client you've manually configured.
tips.codeSnippet:
<domain-config>
    <domain includeSubdomains="true">api.example.com</domain>
    <pin-set expiration="2027-06-01">
        <pin digest="SHA-256">AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA=</pin>
        <pin digest="SHA-256">BBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBB=</pin>
    </pin-set>
</domain-config>

tips.title: Set an expiration date on a pin-set as a built-in safety valve
tips.content:
A pin-set with no expiration keeps enforcing pinning indefinitely, even
if your app is never updated again — if the pinned key is ever rotated
without a corresponding app update reaching every user, those un-updated
installs are permanently locked out of your API with no recovery path
short of a forced reinstall.

The expiration attribute makes Network Security Config automatically stop
enforcing pinning after the given date, falling back to normal
certificate validation — this bounds the worst-case impact of a forgotten
or delayed pin rotation instead of leaving it open-ended.
tips.codeSnippet:
<pin-set expiration="2027-01-01"> <!-- pinning enforcement automatically lapses after this date -->
    <pin digest="SHA-256">AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA=</pin>
</pin-set>

tips.title: Pinning an intermediate CA trades some security specificity for a much lower maintenance burden
tips.content:
Pinning the leaf server certificate's key gives the tightest possible
security guarantee, but ties every app release to that exact leaf key —
any leaf rotation, planned or emergency, requires a coordinated app
update.

Pinning your CA's intermediate certificate instead lets your backend team
rotate leaf certificates freely (a routine, frequent operation) without
touching the app at all, while still meaningfully restricting which CA
can issue certificates trusted by your app — a reasonable middle ground
between leaf pinning's precision and no pinning's lack of protection.
tips.codeSnippet:
<!-- Pinning the intermediate CA's key — leaf certs can rotate freely underneath it -->
<pin-set>
    <pin digest="SHA-256">INTERMEDIATE_CA_SPKI_HASH=</pin>
</pin-set>

tips.title: Extract a certificate's SPKI pin value with openssl before hardcoding it
tips.content:
Manually computing an SPKI hash by hand or trusting a third-party pin-
generator tool of unknown provenance is both error-prone and a poor
security practice for something this sensitive.

openssl's own commands can extract a live server's certificate and
compute its SPKI SHA-256 hash directly, giving you a pin value you can
verify yourself rather than trusting an intermediate tool — this should
be run against the actual production endpoint, not a staging environment
which may use a different certificate entirely.
tips.codeSnippet:
openssl s_client -connect api.example.com:443 -servername api.example.com < /dev/null 2>/dev/null \
  | openssl x509 -pubkey -noout \
  | openssl pkey -pubin -outform der \
  | openssl dgst -sha256 -binary \
  | openssl enc -base64
# output is the sha256/... pin value to hardcode or declare in XML

tips.title: Pinning supplements chain validation — it doesn't replace it
tips.content:
Certificate pinning is an additional check layered on top of standard
TLS certificate chain validation, not a substitute for it — the system
still verifies the certificate is validly signed, unexpired, and matches
the hostname; pinning adds the further requirement that the key also
matches a specific expected value.

A misconception is that pinning alone is sufficient security, leading to
weakened chain validation elsewhere (a permissive TrustManager, say)
under the assumption pinning covers it — both layers need to be correctly
in place, since disabling standard validation still allows any pinned-
matching key to be presented via a different, otherwise-invalid chain in
some misconfigurations.
tips.codeSnippet:
// Pinning is layered ON TOP of default validation — don't also weaken the TrustManager:
val client = OkHttpClient.Builder()
    .certificatePinner(pinner) // additional check
    .build() // default X509TrustManager still performs full chain validation underneath

tips.title: includeSubdomains scopes a pin-set correctly across an entire domain family
tips.content:
Declaring a domain-config for just "example.com" without
includeSubdomains applies the pin-set only to that exact host, leaving
requests to api.example.com or cdn.example.com completely unpinned and
vulnerable — a common oversight when an app talks to several subdomains
under the same parent domain.

Setting includeSubdomains="true" extends the same pin-set to every
subdomain automatically, which is usually the intended behavior when all
subdomains share the same certificate infrastructure — but it should be
omitted deliberately if some subdomains genuinely use different,
unrelated certificates that shouldn't be pinned the same way.
tips.codeSnippet:
<domain-config>
    <domain includeSubdomains="true">example.com</domain> <!-- covers api., cdn., etc. -->
    <pin-set>
        <pin digest="SHA-256">AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA=</pin>
    </pin-set>
</domain-config>

tips.title: report-uri gives you visibility into pin failures happening in the field
tips.content:
Without any reporting mechanism, a pin validation failure on a user's
device is invisible to you — you have no way to distinguish a rare,
legitimate active MITM attack from a botched certificate rotation
affecting your whole user base, both of which look identical from the
app's perspective (requests just start failing).

Network Security Config's report-uri attribute on a pin-set makes the
platform automatically POST a structured report to your specified
endpoint whenever pin validation fails, giving you production visibility
into pinning failures without needing to build custom client-side
reporting logic yourself.
tips.codeSnippet:
<pin-set expiration="2027-01-01">
    <pin digest="SHA-256">AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA=</pin>
</pin-set>
<!-- report-uri is declared at the domain-config level in newer API levels -->
<trustkit-config reportUri="https://reports.example.com/pin-failures" />

tips.title: Verify pinning actually blocks interception by testing it against a MITM proxy tool
tips.content:
It's easy to configure pinning, see the app work normally, and assume
it's correctly protecting against interception — but a normal test run
only proves requests succeed against your real server, not that pinning
would actually reject a different, attacker-controlled certificate.

Deliberately pointing the app at a local interception proxy (Charles,
mitmproxy, Burp Suite) with its own self-signed root CA installed on the
test device is the only way to confirm pinning genuinely rejects an
unexpected certificate — if requests still succeed through the proxy,
pinning isn't actually working as configured.

tips.title: Multi-CDN or multi-origin backends need a distinct pin set per host, not one shared pin
tips.content:
An app that talks to several distinct backend hosts (an API domain, a
separate CDN domain, a third-party auth provider) can't use one single
pin value across all of them, since each host almost certainly has its
own independent certificate and key.

Each domain-config block (or each CertificatePinner.add() call) is scoped
to its own specific hostname — declaring pins for one host doesn't
protect requests to a different host at all, so every distinct backend
origin the app talks to needs its own pin set declared and maintained
independently.
tips.codeSnippet:
CertificatePinner.Builder()
    .add("api.example.com", "sha256/API_HOST_PIN=")
    .add("cdn.example.com", "sha256/CDN_HOST_PIN=") // separate pin for a separate host
    .add("auth.thirdparty.com", "sha256/AUTH_PROVIDER_PIN=")
    .build()

tips.title: Not every networking library or protocol supports pinning out of the box — verify before assuming
tips.content:
OkHttp (and by extension Retrofit, which uses OkHttp underneath) has
first-class CertificatePinner support, but other networking stacks —
some coroutine-native Ktor engines, raw HttpURLConnection, some
WebSocket libraries — may need a custom TrustManager wired in manually to
achieve the same protection, or may not support fine-grained pinning at
all.

Relying on Network Security Config for pinning sidesteps this
inconsistency somewhat, since it applies at the platform TLS layer
regardless of which HTTP client library issues the request — but it's
still worth explicitly verifying pinning is actually active for every
networking path an app uses, including any third-party SDKs making their
own independent network calls.

tips.title: Coordinate pin updates with your backend team's certificate rotation calendar
tips.content:
Certificate pinning creates a hard dependency between your mobile app's
release cadence and your backend infrastructure's certificate lifecycle
— a backend team rotating certificates without informing mobile
engineering (or on a shorter notice than your app's release/rollout
timeline allows) breaks every un-updated app install the moment the
rotation goes live.

Establishing a shared calendar or notification process between backend
and mobile teams, with pin updates shipped and given time to roll out to
most of the user base well before a planned rotation actually happens,
avoids an entirely preventable self-inflicted outage.

tips.title: Pinning alone doesn't stop a bypass via Frida or objection on a rooted or instrumented device
tips.content:
Certificate pinning defends against network-level interception — it says
nothing about an attacker who can modify the app's own running process,
which is exactly what tools like Frida (with scripts such as
ssl-pinning-bypass) or objection are built to do: hooking the pinning
check itself at runtime and forcing it to always pass, regardless of the
actual certificate presented.

Pinning should be paired with root detection, debugger/instrumentation
detection, and runtime application self-protection (RASP) measures for
any app handling genuinely sensitive data — pinning defends the network
path, while these additional measures defend against an attacker who has
already gained control of the device or process itself.

tips.title: A remote pinning kill switch must be signed and verified, never a bare feature flag
tips.content:
A remote config flag that can disable pinning entirely (useful for an
emergency where a pin rotation goes wrong and locks out your whole user
base) is itself a serious attack surface if it's just a plain, unsigned
value fetched over the network — an attacker performing an active MITM
attack could simply serve a fake 'disable pinning' response and defeat
the protection entirely, which is the exact attack pinning exists to
prevent.

If a kill switch is genuinely necessary, the config response enabling it
must itself be cryptographically signed with a key embedded in the app,
and verified before being honored — an unsigned kill switch delivered
over a connection an attacker controls is a backdoor around your own
security control.

tips.title: Unit test pin validation against a local server presenting a known certificate
tips.content:
Manually testing pinning against production or a live MITM proxy is
valuable but slow and not something you'd want in a CI pipeline running
on every commit — pinning logic can still be exercised automatically
with a local test server.

MockWebServer (or a similar embedded test server) configured with
HandshakeCertificates to present a known, self-generated test
certificate lets you write an automated test asserting that a request
with the correct pin succeeds and one with a mismatched pin fails —
catching a pinning regression in CI rather than in production.
tips.codeSnippet:
val serverCert = HeldCertificate.Builder().build()
val serverCertificates = HandshakeCertificates.Builder().heldCertificate(serverCert).build()
val mockWebServer = MockWebServer().apply { useHttps(serverCertificates.sslSocketFactory(), false) }

val clientPinner = CertificatePinner.Builder()
    .add(mockWebServer.hostName, CertificatePinner.pin(serverCert.certificate))
    .build()
// assert requests succeed with the matching pin, fail with a wrong one

tips.title: Hardcoded pins in an APK can be located and patched out — pinning isn't tamper-proof by itself
tips.content:
A pin value embedded as a plain string literal in your app's code is
trivially findable via static analysis (JADX, grep across decompiled
smali) and, on a device where the app can be repackaged and re-signed for
sideloading, the actual pinning check or the pin value itself can be
patched out entirely — pinning defends the honest network path, not
against a determined attacker willing to modify and reinstall your app.

Obfuscating pin-checking logic (via DexGuard/R8), combined with app
signature verification at runtime (rejecting execution if the app's own
signing certificate doesn't match the expected one), raises the bar
against this class of tampering, though no client-side protection can
fully eliminate it against a sufficiently motivated attacker.

tips.title: Always use SHA-256 for pin hashes — never MD5 or SHA-1
tips.content:
MD5 and SHA-1 are both cryptographically broken for collision resistance
— a sufficiently motivated attacker could theoretically construct a
different key that produces the same hash value, defeating the whole
point of pinning against a specific known-good key.

SHA-256 is the standard, currently-secure choice used by both OkHttp's
CertificatePinner (the sha256/ prefix is mandatory, not optional) and
Network Security Config's digest="SHA-256" attribute — there's no valid
reason to use a weaker hash for a security-critical pin value.

tips.title: Give users a grace period after a required pin update, rather than hard-failing immediately
tips.content:
Enforcing a new pin set the instant it's added to a release forces every
single user onto the exact same rollout timeline as your app store
release — but app store rollouts are gradual and app updates aren't
instant for every user, so a hard cutover risks breaking the app for
users who haven't updated yet if the old pin is dropped too aggressively.

A staged approach — shipping the new pin alongside the old one for
several releases, then only removing the old pin once adoption metrics
show the vast majority of active users have updated — avoids an abrupt
breakage for the tail of users still on an older version during the
transition window.
tips.codeSnippet:
CertificatePinner.Builder()
    .add("api.example.com", "sha256/OLD_PIN_STILL_VALID=") // kept during the transition window
    .add("api.example.com", "sha256/NEW_PIN=")
    .build()
// remove OLD_PIN only in a later release, once adoption of this release is high enough

tips.title: Network Security Config pinning also covers WebView traffic; OkHttp's CertificatePinner does not
tips.content:
An app using an embedded WebView (for an in-app browser, a hybrid
feature, an OAuth login page) makes its own independent network
connections that never pass through your app's configured OkHttpClient
at all — OkHttp-level pinning simply has no effect on that traffic,
leaving it fully exposed to interception even in an app that otherwise
pins correctly.

Network Security Config's pinning enforcement operates at the platform's
TLS layer, which WebView traffic does go through — making it the correct
choice (or a necessary addition alongside OkHttp pinning) for any app
that embeds WebView-based content touching sensitive endpoints.
tips.codeSnippet:
<!-- Network Security Config protects WebView requests too, unlike OkHttp-only pinning -->
<domain-config>
    <domain includeSubdomains="true">login.example.com</domain> <!-- e.g. an OAuth page loaded in a WebView -->
    <pin-set expiration="2027-01-01">
        <pin digest="SHA-256">AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA=</pin>
    </pin-set>
</domain-config>

tips.title: Pin validation failures need different user-facing messaging than ordinary network errors
tips.content:
Surfacing a pin failure to the user as a generic 'Network error, please
try again' message invites them to retry repeatedly against what might
be an active attack, and gives your support team no way to distinguish
real connectivity issues from a security event when users report the
problem.

A distinct, clear message for pin failures specifically (something like
'Unable to verify a secure connection' rather than a generic timeout
message) sets correct user expectations that this isn't a transient
issue solvable by retrying on a different network, and internal logging
should tag pin failures separately from ordinary timeouts or DNS errors
for proper triage.

tips.title: Network Security Config blocks cleartext traffic declaratively, without touching code
tips.content:
Even with HTTPS used everywhere intentionally, a single accidental HTTP
request (a misconfigured SDK, a stray debug endpoint) sends data in plain
text, trivially interceptable by anyone on the same network — a classic
and very common MITM entry point that has nothing to do with TLS
weaknesses at all.

A network_security_config.xml with
cleartextTrafficPermitted="false" makes the OS itself refuse any HTTP
connection app-wide, turning an accidental cleartext request into an
immediate, loud failure during development instead of a silent security
hole in production.
tips.codeSnippet:
<!-- res/xml/network_security_config.xml -->
<network-security-config>
    <base-config cleartextTrafficPermitted="false" />
</network-security-config>

<!-- AndroidManifest.xml -->
<application android:networkSecurityConfig="@xml/network_security_config" />

tips.title: Distrust user and admin-added CA certificates to block the most common MITM proxy attacks
tips.content:
By default on Android 6 and below, apps trust CA certificates a user
installs manually — this is exactly the mechanism MITM interception
tools (Charles, mitmproxy, Burp Suite, and malicious device profiles)
rely on: install their own root CA, then issue fake certificates for any
domain your app connects to that your app trusts implicitly.

Restricting trust to system-preinstalled CAs only (excluding user-
installed ones) closes this attack vector entirely for a normal user
device, since an attacker would need to compromise the actual system CA
store, a far higher bar than getting a user to install one profile.
tips.codeSnippet:
<network-security-config>
    <base-config>
        <trust-anchors>
            <certificates src="system" /> <!-- only system CAs, no user-added ones -->
        </trust-anchors>
    </base-config>
</network-security-config>

tips.title: debug-overrides trusting user CAs must never leak into a release build
tips.content:
Trusting user-installed CAs is genuinely useful during development,
since tools like Charles or mitmproxy need to intercept your own app's
traffic for debugging — Network Security Config's <debug-overrides>
block is designed exactly for this, applying only when
android:debuggable="true".

The risk is a misconfiguration that puts the same trust settings in
<base-config> instead of <debug-overrides>, or a release build that's
accidentally left debuggable — either mistake ships a build to real
users that trusts arbitrary user-installed certificates, silently
reopening the exact MITM vector the production config was meant to
close.
tips.codeSnippet:
<network-security-config>
    <base-config cleartextTrafficPermitted="false">
        <trust-anchors><certificates src="system" /></trust-anchors>
    </base-config>
    <debug-overrides> <!-- only active when android:debuggable="true" -->
        <trust-anchors><certificates src="user" /></trust-anchors>
    </debug-overrides>
</network-security-config>

tips.title: A custom TrustManager that trusts every certificate defeats TLS entirely
tips.content:
It's a surprisingly common pattern — usually copy-pasted from a
StackOverflow answer meant to 'fix' an SSL error during development —
to implement an X509TrustManager whose checkServerTrusted() method does
nothing, silently accepting any certificate presented, including one
from an active MITM attacker.

This single mistake makes the app's TLS connections cryptographically
meaningless: an attacker on the network path can present literally any
self-signed certificate and the app will accept it as valid, defeating
both encryption and authentication guarantees TLS is supposed to
provide.

tips.title: A permissive HostnameVerifier is just as dangerous as a permissive TrustManager
tips.content:
Even with a correctly validated certificate chain, TLS still requires
verifying the certificate's hostname actually matches the server you
intended to connect to — a valid certificate for evil.com presented
during a connection to api.yourapp.com should still fail, since it
proves the attacker controls a different domain, not yours.

Overriding HostnameVerifier.verify() to always return true (another
common 'quick fix' for SSL errors) removes this check entirely, allowing
an attacker with any valid certificate for any domain to successfully
impersonate your server, even if certificate chain validation itself is
still correctly configured.

tips.title: Certificate Transparency checks catch mis-issued certificates that pinning alone can miss
tips.content:
Certificate pinning protects against a specific known-good certificate
being swapped for an attacker's — but it assumes you've already pinned
the correct certificate; it does nothing to detect if a Certificate
Authority is tricked or compromised into issuing a *legitimate-looking*
certificate for your domain to someone else before you've pinned
against it.

Certificate Transparency requires CAs to publish every issued
certificate to public, auditable logs — verifying a server's certificate
includes valid Signed Certificate Timestamps from those logs adds a
layer of detection for fraudulently issued certificates that a pure
pinning strategy, focused only on the certificates you already know
about, wouldn't catch on its own.
tips.codeSnippet:
// OkHttp doesn't verify CT natively — use a library or a CertificateTransparencyInterceptor
val client = OkHttpClient.Builder()
    .addNetworkInterceptor(certificateTransparencyInterceptor { +"*.example.com" })
    .build()

tips.title: Enforce a minimum TLS version and disable legacy protocols explicitly
tips.content:
Older TLS versions (TLS 1.0, 1.1) and SSL entirely have known
cryptographic weaknesses (BEAST, POODLE, and others) that can allow an
active network attacker to downgrade or partially decrypt a connection
that should otherwise be secure — a server or client that still
negotiates these older protocols is vulnerable even if certificate
validation itself is correct.

Explicitly restricting ConnectionSpec to modern TLS versions only (1.2+,
ideally 1.3) prevents a downgrade attack from succeeding, since the
client itself refuses to fall back to a weaker protocol even if a MITM
attacker tries to force renegotiation to one.
tips.codeSnippet:
val spec = ConnectionSpec.Builder(ConnectionSpec.MODERN_TLS)
    .tlsVersions(TlsVersion.TLS_1_3, TlsVersion.TLS_1_2)
    .build()

val client = OkHttpClient.Builder()
    .connectionSpecs(listOf(spec)) // refuses to negotiate down to older, weaker TLS
    .build()

tips.title: Use overlapping pin sets to survive certificate rotation without a forced app update
tips.content:
A single active pin plus one backup pin still creates a hard dependency
on your app update cadence — if the server's certificate is rotated
before users have updated to a build with the new pin, every un-updated
install starts failing every request, which looks identical to (and
could mask) an actual MITM attack in your monitoring.

Maintaining pins for the current certificate, the next planned
rotation's certificate, and a longer-lived backup root/intermediate all
simultaneously gives a rotation window where old and new app versions
both keep working, without ever needing to temporarily disable pinning
to avoid breaking users.
tips.codeSnippet:
val pinner = CertificatePinner.Builder()
    .add("api.example.com", "sha256/CURRENT_CERT_PIN=")
    .add("api.example.com", "sha256/NEXT_ROTATION_CERT_PIN=") // added ahead of the actual rotation
    .add("api.example.com", "sha256/LONG_LIVED_ROOT_PIN=")
    .build()

tips.title: An unexpectedly short or altered certificate chain can signal an active interception proxy
tips.content:
A legitimate TLS connection to your server presents a predictable
certificate chain (leaf, intermediate(s), and implicitly the trusted
root) — an interception proxy sitting in the middle re-signs traffic
with its own certificates, which often produces a chain with a different
length, issuer, or validity period than what a genuine connection
normally shows.

Inspecting the negotiated certificate chain at runtime (via
HandshakeCertificates or an OkHttp interceptor) and comparing it against
an expected shape — issuer CN, chain depth, validity window — gives an
additional runtime signal for detecting an active proxy, layered on top
of (not replacing) certificate pinning itself.

tips.title: Pin failures should fail closed and be reported, never silently retried without pinning
tips.content:
A common but dangerous mistake is catching a CertificatePinner
validation failure and quietly retrying the request without pinning
enabled, 'just to keep the app working' — this converts a hard security
boundary into a soft one an attacker can trigger on demand, since
triggering a pin failure is exactly what an active MITM attack does.

A pin validation failure should abort the request entirely, surface a
clear error to the user (not a generic network error that invites
retrying), and ideally report the failure to a monitoring backend — a
genuine pin failure in production is a strong signal of either an active
attack or an unplanned certificate rotation, both of which need visibility,
not silent bypass.

tips.title: Keystore-backed keys never exist in extractable form, even to your own app
tips.content:
A key generated inside the Android Keystore is created and used entirely
inside secure hardware (a Trusted Execution Environment or, on supported
devices, a dedicated StrongBox security chip) — your app only ever holds
a reference (an alias) to the key, never the raw key material itself.

This means even a full compromise of your app's process — a debugger
attached, memory dumped, the APK reverse engineered — cannot extract the
actual key bytes, since they were never present in application memory to
begin with; the app can only ask the secure hardware to perform
encrypt/decrypt/sign operations on its behalf.

tips.title: KeyGenParameterSpec explicitly declares every property a Keystore key is allowed to use
tips.content:
Unlike a plain in-memory key, a Keystore key's algorithm, block mode,
padding, and permitted purposes (ENCRYPT, DECRYPT, SIGN, VERIFY) are all
locked in at generation time via KeyGenParameterSpec — the key simply
refuses to be used in any way not explicitly declared upfront, at the
secure hardware level.

This is a deliberate security property, not a limitation to work around:
if a key is only generated with PURPOSE_ENCRYPT, no code path in your app
(or an attacker's, if compromised) can misuse it for signing, since the
hardware itself enforces the restriction.
tips.codeSnippet:
val keyGenSpec = KeyGenParameterSpec.Builder(
    "payment_token_key",
    KeyProperties.PURPOSE_ENCRYPT or KeyProperties.PURPOSE_DECRYPT
)
    .setBlockModes(KeyProperties.BLOCK_MODE_GCM)
    .setEncryptionPaddings(KeyProperties.ENCRYPTION_PADDING_NONE)
    .setKeySize(256)
    .build()

tips.title: Never reuse an IV with the same AES/GCM Keystore key — store it alongside the ciphertext
tips.content:
AES/GCM's security guarantee breaks catastrophically if the same
(key, IV) pair is ever used to encrypt two different plaintexts — an
attacker who observes two ciphertexts sharing an IV can potentially
recover both plaintexts, defeating the encryption entirely.

The Keystore Cipher generates a fresh random IV automatically each time
you call init() for encryption, but it's your responsibility to store
that IV (it's not secret, just needs to be unique per encryption)
alongside the ciphertext so decryption can retrieve it — losing track of
which IV was used for which ciphertext makes that data unrecoverable.
tips.codeSnippet:
val cipher = Cipher.getInstance("AES/GCM/NoPadding")
cipher.init(Cipher.ENCRYPT_MODE, secretKey) // fresh random IV generated internally
val iv = cipher.iv // must be persisted alongside the ciphertext, per encryption
val ciphertext = cipher.doFinal(plaintext)

val stored = iv + ciphertext // IV prepended — needed again for decryption

tips.title: setUserAuthenticationRequired ties key usage to biometric or device-credential verification
tips.content:
By default, a Keystore key is usable by your app any time the app itself
is running, with no additional user gate beyond normal app access.

setUserAuthenticationRequired(true) makes the secure hardware itself
refuse to perform any operation with that key until the user has
recently authenticated with biometrics or a device PIN/pattern/password —
this enforcement happens at the hardware level, so it can't be bypassed
by an attacker who's compromised your app's code but hasn't defeated the
device's own biometric/lock-screen security.
tips.codeSnippet:
val spec = KeyGenParameterSpec.Builder("secure_key", KeyProperties.PURPOSE_DECRYPT)
    .setBlockModes(KeyProperties.BLOCK_MODE_GCM)
    .setEncryptionPaddings(KeyProperties.ENCRYPTION_PADDING_NONE)
    .setUserAuthenticationRequired(true) // hardware refuses use without recent auth
    .build()

tips.title: setInvalidatedByBiometricEnrollment auto-revokes a key when biometrics change
tips.content:
If a device's enrolled fingerprints or face data change (a new fingerprint
added, all biometrics cleared) after a biometric-gated key was created,
that could mean a different physical person now has biometric access to
a key originally gated to the legitimate owner — a real security
concern for high-sensitivity keys.

setInvalidatedByBiometricEnrollment(true) (the default for user-
authentication-required keys) makes the key permanently unusable the
moment biometric enrollment changes, forcing the app to detect this
(via a KeyPermanentlyInvalidatedException) and have the user re-
authenticate through a proper account-level flow to regenerate the key.

tips.title: Key attestation cryptographically proves a key is genuinely hardware-backed
tips.content:
An app can't simply trust its own claim that a key is Keystore-protected
— on some older or lower-end devices, the 'Android Keystore' provider
falls back to a software-only implementation instead of genuine secure
hardware, and a compromised OS could theoretically lie about which
implementation is in use.

Key attestation generates a certificate chain, signed by a hardware root
of trust, that a backend server can independently verify — proving the
key genuinely lives in secure hardware (and details like whether it's
TEE or StrongBox-backed) without trusting the app's own self-report,
which matters for high-assurance scenarios like mobile payment
provisioning.
tips.codeSnippet:
val spec = KeyGenParameterSpec.Builder("attested_key", KeyProperties.PURPOSE_SIGN)
    .setDigests(KeyProperties.DIGEST_SHA256)
    .setAttestationChallenge(challengeFromServer) // server-provided nonce, prevents replay
    .build()
// resulting certificate chain is sent to the backend for independent verification

tips.title: StrongBox offers stronger isolation than a TEE, but isn't available on every device
tips.content:
A Trusted Execution Environment (TEE) runs in an isolated mode on the
main processor, offering strong isolation from a compromised OS but
still sharing the same physical chip — StrongBox is a separate, dedicated
security chip entirely, offering protection even against certain physical
hardware attacks a TEE alone can't fully resist.

StrongBox is only present on a subset of higher-end devices, so
setIsStrongBoxBacked(true) can throw StrongBoxUnavailableException on
devices without it — code requesting StrongBox for its highest-
sensitivity keys needs an explicit fallback path to a regular
TEE-backed key rather than assuming availability.

tips.title: Keystore keys do not survive app reinstall, uninstall, or most backup/restore flows
tips.content:
Keystore keys are tied to the specific app installation and the specific
device's secure hardware state — uninstalling and reinstalling the app
generates a fresh Keystore entry namespace, meaning any data encrypted
with the old key (like a locally cached auth token) becomes permanently
unrecoverable, not just temporarily inaccessible.

Android's auto-backup and Google's Backup/Restore services explicitly
exclude Keystore-backed key material by design (it can't be safely
exported), so an app relying on Keystore encryption for locally-cached
data must treat that data as ephemeral and re-derivable, not as a
permanent store — critical data belongs on a server, with the Keystore
key only protecting a local cache or session token.

tips.title: Prefer per-operation BiometricPrompt.CryptoObject auth over long validity windows
tips.content:
setUserAuthenticationValidityDurationSeconds(n) allows a key to be used
repeatedly for n seconds after a single successful authentication —
convenient, but it widens the window during which a device left unlocked
or briefly accessible by someone else could misuse the key without
re-prompting.

Binding the key to a BiometricPrompt.CryptoObject instead (with no
validity duration set, or duration -1) requires a fresh biometric/device-
credential prompt for every single use of the key, which is the stronger
default for genuinely sensitive operations like authorizing a payment or
decrypting a private key.

tips.title: Use separate key aliases per purpose instead of one shared Keystore key
tips.content:
Reusing a single Keystore key across unrelated purposes (encrypting
tokens, signing requests, protecting a local database) couples their
security lifecycles together — invalidating or rotating the key for one
purpose (say, after biometric enrollment changes) forces you to also
lose access to everything else protected by that same key.

Generating a distinct key alias per logical purpose
("token_encryption_key", "request_signing_key") lets each be rotated,
invalidated, or configured (different auth requirements, different
StrongBox usage) independently, and limits the blast radius if one key's
usage needs to be revoked.
